You return to your plate. Dev waits a moment, then accepts that answer without pressing and carries the equipment case upstairs.

The sounds of the building separate again: cutlery at the table, running water in the kitchen, Martin’s voice muffled beyond the auditorium doors and the soft tread of Dev crossing the landing overhead.

You finish the stew and the last of your pie. Jo leaves your plate alone until you set down your fork, then collects it with the others.

“Now,” she says to Nell, “it can become a meeting if it absolutely has to.”

Nell turns over the envelope. “Five minutes.”

She runs through immediate jobs rather than making speeches. A crockery delivery is due Wednesday. Jo’s menu should go to print the same afternoon, provided her final costings hold. She is keeping her lunch van’s Friday route through October, so the cinema cannot expect her before two on Fridays.

“I’ve written that down in three places,” Nell says.

“Good. It’ll survive contact with your optimism.”

Owen dries a stack of bowls at the kitchen hatch while Nell checks another note.

“Thursday,” she says. “I’ve got you ten until four. Foyer labels, counter fittings and whatever opening-week disaster has emerged by then.”

Owen stops with the cloth inside a bowl. Jo continues washing, her back to the table.

“I need to change Thursday,” he says.

Nell looks up. “The whole shift?”

“At least the morning. I’ve been offered an interview at eleven. Exhibition technician at a museum inland.”

The water continues running. From the auditorium comes the click of Rosa’s camera.

“Permanent?” Nell asks.

“That’s the job. This is only the interview.”

“When did you hear?”

“Today. They want an answer by noon Wednesday.”

Nell draws one line through the shift. “Reply tonight. Send me the travel times when you have them, and I’ll move the work.”

“I can make up the hours.”

“We’ll work that out after you know what journey you’re making.”

Owen sets the dried bowl on the counter. His eyes move briefly towards the closed auditorium doors.

“I haven’t told Dad yet. I will.”

“All right,” Nell says. She writes **OWEN—THURS HOLD** and nothing more.

Jo shuts off the tap. She does not look surprised, but she offers no explanation and adds nothing to what Owen has said.

Behind the doors, Martin’s muffled voice rises in protest.

“I’m telling you, it was eighty-seven.”

Rosa answers, clearer because she is nearer the aisle. “The printed programme says March 1988.”

“The programme could be wrong.”

“That’s going in the recording too.”

Bea’s laughter follows.

At the table, Nell folds the envelope once and slips it into her pocket. Owen begins carrying the remaining dishes into the kitchen, and Jo makes room for him at the draining board. Upstairs, a case latch snaps shut, followed by the steady whir of equipment in the booth.
